etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French prospectif, from Late Latin prospectivus. See more at English prospect.

definitions.definition: Likely or expected to happen or become.
Anticipated in the near or far future.

quote.citation: 1968, Herold Jacob Wiens, “I-CH’ANG”, in Encyclopedia Britannica‎[1], volume 11, →LCCN, →OCLC, page 1054, column 1:
quote.text: A short distance above I-ch’ang is the prospective site of a hydroelectric dam that has vast promise for the industrialization of central China.

definitions.definition: Of or relating to a prospect; furnishing a prospect.

quote.citation: 1626 (date written), John Milton, “At a Vacation Exercise in the Colledge, […]”, in Poems, &c. upon Several Occasions, London:  […]  Tho[mas] Dring […], published 1673, →OCLC, page 67:
quote.text: And in times long and dark Proſpective Glaſs / Fore-ſaw what future dayes ſhould bring to paſs,

definitions.definition: Looking forward in time; acting with foresight.

quote.citation: 1668-1690, Josiah Child, A new discourse of trade
quote.text: The French king, and the king of Sweden are  […] circumspect, industrious, and prospective, too, in this affair.

definitions.definition: (medicine, of research) A study that starts with the present situation and follows participants into the future
(grammar) Indicating grammatically an activity about to begin.
(obsolete) The scene before or around, in time or in space; view; prospect.

quote.citation: 1642, Henry Wotton, A Short View of the Life and Death of George Villiers:
quote.text: the whole Scene of affairs was changed from Spain to France there now lay the prospective

quote.citation: 1613 March 2 (first performance), Francis Beaumont, “The Masque of the Inner-Temple and Gray’s Inn, Gray’s Inn and the Inner-Temple; […]”, in The Dramatic Works of Ben Jonson, and Beaumont and Fletcher: […], volume IV, London:  […]  John Stockdale, […], published 1811, →OCLC, page 573, column 2:
quote.text: [T]hey [two pavillions] were trimmed on the inside with rich armour and military furniture, hanged up as upon the walls; and behind the tents there were represented, in prospective, the tops of divers other tents, as if it had been a camp.

definitions.definition: (informal, often plural) A prospective (potential) member, student, employee, date, partner, etc.

quote.citation: 2006, Verve: The Spirit of Today's Woman, volume 14, numbers 4-6, page 114:
quote.text: At the moment, meeting interesting, 'could be, maybe not' prospectives around the globe keeps her entertained.
